## subject_definitions

<Subject 1> is the target character defined by <Picture 1>: a stylized young woman with very long silver-white hair, an elegant partial updo, red and black hair ornaments, light-colored eyes, a white off-shoulder upper garment with long flowing sleeves, a black-and-red waist piece, a layered black-and-red skirt with hanging decorative elements, and black high-heeled ankle boots.

<Picture 1> defines character identity and appearance only. It does not define motion, pose, camera, framing, or background.

<Subject 2> is the target environment defined by <Picture 2>: a nighttime traditional Chinese garden courtyard with classical Chinese architecture, a circular moon gate, pavilion structures, blooming pink-red flowering trees, red lanterns, a bright full moon, wet reflective stone pavement, deep blue-black night tones, and subtle atmospheric mist.

<Picture 2> is the exclusive and persistent visual reference for the entire environment and background.

<Subject 3> is a high-quality stylized 3D anime game-character rendering style.

<Video 1> defines character motion, pose, timing, camera movement, framing, camera trajectory, and temporal composition only.

<Video 2> is synchronized frame-by-frame with <Video 1> and defines depth geometry only: subject-to-camera distance, apparent scale, perspective, foreground-background depth relationships, and spatial movement.

Neither <Video 1> nor <Video 2> defines environment appearance.


## summary

Replace the original person in <Video 1> with <Subject 1>.

Completely replace the original environment with the environment defined by <Picture 2> before the first generated frame.

Strictly reproduce the character motion and camera behavior from <Video 1>.

Use <Video 2> to preserve correct subject distance, scale, perspective, and spatial depth.

Reference roles:

<Picture 1> = character appearance.
<Picture 2> = environment appearance and environment identity.
<Video 1> = motion and camera behavior.
<Video 2> = depth and spatial geometry.

The environment identity must remain locked to <Picture 2> from the first frame to the final frame.


## opening_environment_lock

From the very first generated frame, the entire visible environment must already match <Picture 2>.

Do NOT begin with the original environment from <Video 1>.

Do NOT gradually transition from the source background into <Picture 2>.

Do NOT use <Video 1> to initialize the environment appearance.

At frame 1, <Subject 1> must already exist inside the nighttime traditional Chinese garden defined by <Picture 2>.

Use <Picture 2> as the persistent environment anchor from the first frame to the final frame.

The original background from <Video 1> must never appear, including at the beginning.


## environment_persistence

The generated environment must remain the SAME physical location throughout the entire sequence.

The environment identity must remain locked to <Picture 2> during all camera movement, camera rotation, framing changes, viewpoint changes, and newly revealed areas.

During camera rotation, the environment must still remain the SAME nighttime traditional Chinese garden courtyard defined by <Picture 2>.

Do NOT restore the original background from <Video 1>.

Do NOT mix the source environment with the target environment.

Do NOT switch to another location.

Do NOT create a temporary substitute background.

Do NOT create a transitional background.

Do NOT invent a new environment that is inconsistent with <Picture 2>.

If the camera reveals previously unseen areas, generate them as a natural continuation of the SAME environment defined by <Picture 2>.

Treat <Picture 2> as defining the identity of the whole surrounding environment, not just one flat image.

All newly visible regions must preserve the same architectural language, mood, lighting, materials, and atmosphere as <Picture 2>.

Maintain consistent classical Chinese architecture, circular moon gate, pavilion structures, flowering trees, red lanterns, wet reflective stone pavement, moonlight, deep blue-black night tones, subtle mist, vegetation, materials, lighting, and color palette throughout the entire sequence.

The environment may change in viewpoint, but it must never change in identity.

Camera motion changes how the environment is viewed, but it must never change what environment it is.

The background must remain stable, persistent, and scene-consistent throughout the full video.


## detailed_description

Strictly follow <Video 1> frame-by-frame.

Preserve the source pose progression, body orientation, limb trajectories, spatial movement, timing, speed, motion rhythm, camera trajectory, framing, camera rotation, and composition.

Strictly follow the spatial geometry from <Video 2>.

Maintain the subject-to-camera distance, apparent subject scale, perspective, and foreground-background depth relationships indicated by <Video 2>.

When the source character moves toward the camera, reproduce the corresponding depth change.

When the source character moves away from the camera, reproduce the corresponding depth change.

When the source character remains at a stable distance, keep the generated character at a stable distance.

Do not autonomously zoom in or out.

Do not autonomously dolly forward or backward.

Do not autonomously widen the shot.

Do not autonomously reframe or recenter the character.

Do not autonomously change focal length, field of view, camera height, or viewing angle.

Completely discard the original environment appearance from <Video 1>.

Do not preserve or reconstruct the original background, scenery, architecture, objects, textures, colors, or environmental lighting from <Video 1>.

Do not render or reproduce the grayscale visual appearance of <Video 2>.

Use <Video 2> only as spatial and depth guidance.

Render the entire visible environment according to <Picture 2>.

The environment must adapt naturally to the camera motion from <Video 1> and the depth geometry from <Video 2>.

The camera and character motion must NOT adapt to the composition of <Picture 2>.

<Picture 1> controls WHO the character is.

<Picture 2> controls WHERE the character is and what the surrounding world looks like.

<Video 1> controls HOW the character moves and HOW the camera moves.

<Video 2> controls HOW FAR the character is from the camera and HOW spatial depth evolves.

Character appearance must come from <Picture 1>.

Environment appearance and environment identity must come from <Picture 2>.

Motion and camera behavior must come from <Video 1>.

Spatial geometry must come from <Video 2>.

Keep these responsibilities separated throughout the entire sequence.

Motion fidelity and depth fidelity are important, but environment identity must remain stable at all times.

No additional characters.

No invented actions.

No pose substitution.

No motion reinterpretation.

No autonomous camera movement.

No autonomous reframing.

No unintended zoom.

No original background from <Video 1>.

No visible depth-map appearance.

No scene switching.

No background switching.

No environment drift.

Maintain strict temporal synchronization between <Video 1> and <Video 2> from the first frame to the final frame.


## overall_soundscape

Inherited from <Video 1>.


## non_diegetic_music

Inherited from <Video 1>.
